meta.title: Sample Northeast land-use reading rules
meta.limitations: Educational samples only. Not evaluated against live GIS. Stone walls alone never prove pasture. Regional geology and settlement patterns differ. Fire, mining, and flood readings stay provisional without maps or records.

rules.title: Agricultural abandonment after pasture cues

if.plainLanguage: If stone walls are present and fence remnants or even-aged tree lines along walls are present…

all.description: Fence remnant or even-aged wall tree line

then.label: Former pasture
then.statementTemplate: This landscape may have regenerated after agricultural abandonment, with stone walls and fence-line trees consistent with historic pasture.
then.plainLanguage: …this landscape may have regenerated after agricultural abandonment; stone walls likely relate to historic pasture enclosure.

evidenceHints: Stone walls used as enclosure rather than only property theater
Fence metal or parallel wall-line of same-age trees
alternatives: Walls may mark hay-field or woodlot boundaries without grazing.
Trees may be planting or tree-lines for wind, not pasture regeneration.
Later logging may mimic even-aged cohorts along edges.
fieldChecks: Follow the wall continuity — pasture walls often enclose shapes, not only straight property lines.
Look for wire staples in older trees along the wall.
Compare understory: thorny or browse-resistant shrubs sometimes linger after grazing.
rules.limitations: Without historic maps or aerials, keep confidence at or below moderate. Do not assert ownership or legal history.
rules.ethicsNotes: Do not dismantle walls or remove artifacts.

rules.title: Stone wall as historic boundary cue

if.plainLanguage: If a stone wall is present without stronger pasture corroboration…

then.label: Stone wall boundary
then.statementTemplate: These stone walls likely indicate a historic boundary — pasture, woodlot, or property division — but wall presence alone does not specify the land use.
then.plainLanguage: …these stone walls likely indicate a historic boundary; look further before naming pasture.

evidenceHints: Presence of dry-laid or rubble stone alignment
alternatives: Former pasture (needs fence, vegetation, or map corroboration).
Woodlot boundary or ornamental landscape feature.
Relocated stone from field clearing without enclosure intent.
fieldChecks: Note wall construction style and height.
Search nearby for cellar holes, lilacs, or orchard spacing.
Ask whether the wall closes a shape or only runs a ridge line.
rules.limitations: This rule teaches humility: walls are evidence of people, not a finished story.

rules.title: Early succession after opening

if.plainLanguage: If dense young stems and open-meadow or shrub signals co-occur…

all.description: Open meadow, shrub thicket, or abrupt edge

then.label: Early succession
then.statementTemplate: Structure here is consistent with early succession after an opening — field abandonment, blowdown, cut, or beaver meadow dynamics may all apply.
then.plainLanguage: …this area may be early succession regenerating after an opening.

evidenceHints: High stem density of pioneer species
Residual open ground or shrub structure
alternatives: Managed early-seral habitat (mowing/cutting regime).
Plantation or seedling release not related to agriculture.
Persistent shrubland community, not transitional forest.
fieldChecks: Estimate stem diameters and canopy height.
Look for stumps vs pasture walls vs beaver cuttings.
Note invasive shrubs that stall succession.
rules.limitations: Successional labels are relative to local climate and seed sources.

rules.title: Beaver influence on wet meadows

if.plainLanguage: If beaver sign is present with seasonal water or drowned timber cues…

then.label: Beaver influence
then.statementTemplate: Wetland and meadow patterning here may reflect beaver influence — dams and water-table changes that create and abandon open habitat over decades.
then.plainLanguage: …beaver activity may help explain wet openings and drowned timber.

evidenceHints: Cuttings, dams, lodges, drowned standing timber
alternatives: Human impoundment or road-related ponding.
Seasonal wetland without beaver.
Historic mill pond remnant.
fieldChecks: Search upstream for dam materials and fresh cuttings.
Note lodge presence and bank dens.
Compare current water level marks on trees.
rules.limitations: Beaver systems cycle; absence of a dam today does not erase recent influence.
rules.ethicsNotes: Observe without destroying lodges or dams; follow local wildlife rules.

rules.title: Glacial deposit cues

if.plainLanguage: If unsorted glacial debris or erratics are present…

then.label: Glacial deposits
then.statementTemplate: Scattered mixed rocks and odd boulders here are consistent with glacial deposits — ice once moved and dropped this material, shaping soils and drainage long before today's forest.
then.plainLanguage: …glacial ice likely left this mix of rock and till.

evidenceHints: Mixed sizes without clear stream sorting
alternatives: Human fill or road spoil mimicking till.
Local bedrock collapse with angular talus instead of rounded erratics.
Outwash sorted by meltwater rather than till.
fieldChecks: Compare rock shapes: rounded far-travelled vs angular local.
Note closed ponds or kettles nearby.
Ask whether soils feel stony and unsorted.
rules.limitations: Regional textbooks and maps refine glacial stories; tags alone stay educational.
rules.ethicsNotes: Do not move erratics from protected sites.

rules.title: Repeated flood activity in a stream valley

if.plainLanguage: If flood debris or scour appears with seasonal standing water or a terrace step…

then.label: Floodplain / repeated flood activity
then.statementTemplate: The stream valley shows signs of repeated flood activity — wrack, scour, or stepped terraces that record high water moving sediment and resetting vegetation.
then.plainLanguage: …this valley likely floods again and again.

alternatives: Single storm damage without a true floodplain.
Beaver ponding raising water without overbank floods.
Road washouts concentrating flow artificially.
fieldChecks: Look for layered fine sediments on the flat.
Note plant species that tolerate brief inundation.
Compare terrace height to today's channel.
rules.limitations: Do not treat this as a flood-insurance determination.
rules.ethicsNotes: Stay off unstable banks; respect private land.

rules.title: Logging history cues

if.plainLanguage: If stumps or skid trails are present with even-aged stems or dense young growth…

then.label: Logging history
then.statementTemplate: Stumps, skid lines, and even-aged regrowth suggest logging history — a cut that reset the stand, not necessarily the end of the forest story.

alternatives: Windthrow followed by salvage looking like a harvest.
Plantation rows rather than natural regeneration.
Fuelwood cutting without commercial logging.
fieldChecks: Count stump diameters and estimate cut age.
Follow compacted corridors for equipment width.
Note species favored after opening.
rules.limitations: Age of stumps matters; old charcoal eras differ from recent cuts.

rules.title: Fire influence cues

if.plainLanguage: If fire scars or char are present with canopy gaps or early succession cues…

then.label: Fire-influenced structure
then.statementTemplate: Char and fire scars with open or young structure suggest fire helped shape this place — sometimes as a reset, sometimes as a patchy thinning that favored certain trees.
then.plainLanguage: …fire likely played a role in how this stand looks.

evidenceHints: Charcoal in soil or on wood
alternatives: Campfire or pile burn with limited stand effect.
Lightning scar without broader burn.
Drought mortality darkening wood without fire.
fieldChecks: Look upslope and downslope for continuous char patterns.
Note sprouting hardwoods vs fire-killed pines.
Ask whether fuels and slope would carry fire.
rules.limitations: Without burn-year records, keep language provisional.
rules.ethicsNotes: Never ignite fuels to 'test' a reading.

rules.title: Mining influence cues

if.plainLanguage: If mining spoil or prospect pits are present…

then.label: Mining influence
then.statementTemplate: Spoil piles or prospect pits suggest mining influence — people moved earth for ore or stone, leaving soils and drainage that vegetation still answers to.
then.plainLanguage: …mining likely left lasting ground scars here.

alternatives: Quarry or borrow pit for road fill, not metal mining.
Root cellars or farm dumps mistaken for pits.
Military or dump trenches.
fieldChecks: Stay outside unstable pits and adits.
Note vegetation that prefers disturbed mineral soils.
Compare spoil rock to local bedrock.
rules.limitations: Safety first — never enter adits. Not a contamination assessment.
rules.ethicsNotes: Do not dig, collect, or enter workings.

rules.title: Infrastructure reshaping topography

if.plainLanguage: If utility corridors, roadcuts, or parallel berms are present…

then.label: Infrastructure edge
then.statementTemplate: Graded benches, road berms, or utility clearings create sharp edges — human infrastructure rewriting light, drainage, and plant communities along a corridor.
then.plainLanguage: …roads or utilities help explain this abrupt edge.

alternatives: Abandoned farm lane still serving as habitat edge.
Natural landslide scarp.
Pipeline ROW vs powerline with different maintenance.
fieldChecks: Follow the line — does it stay ruler-straight?
Note mowing or herbicide maintenance clues.
Watch how water sheds off the cut.
rules.limitations: Do not trespass on active rights-of-way.

rules.title: Kettle / closed depression

if.plainLanguage: If a closed depression without outlet co-occurs with glacial debris cues…

then.label: Kettle depression
then.statementTemplate: A bowl without an outlet, especially amid glacial deposits, may be a kettle — a hollow left where buried ice melted, now holding seasonal water or wetland plants.
then.plainLanguage: …this closed bowl may be a glacial kettle.

alternatives: Sinkhole in carbonate rock (karst).
Human borrow pit.
Beaver meadow abandoned to a wet depression.
fieldChecks: Walk the rim looking for an outlet channel.
Note plant rings that track wetter centers.
Compare with regional kettle lake maps if available.
rules.limitations: Low confidence without regional glacial context.
